title_en: Vanguard’s Plateau Is Exactly What Jack Bogle Wanted
title_zh: Vanguard 见顶走平，正是 Jack Bogle 所愿｜对话 Bloomberg News 记者 Isabel Lee
subtitle_zh: 第一只指数基金50周年之际，Vanguard 市场份额见顶，两位主持与 Isabel Lee 共谈 Bogle 效应。
summary_zh: 本期 Trillions 由 Joel Weber 与 Eric Balchunas 主持，请来 Bloomberg News 跨资产记者 Isabel Lee，围绕'第一只指数基金诞生 50 周年'与'Vanguard 市场份额见顶走平'这两件看似矛盾的事，聊聊所谓的 Bogle 效应（the Bogle effect）。Balchunas 为 Bloomberg Intelligence 写的研究报告发现：Vanguard 占全部基金资产（ETF 加共同基金）的份额在涨到 27% 后基本走平、甚至略降，而 BlackRock、Fidelity 等对手正靠更便宜的产品往上走。他援引创始人 Jack Bogle 1991 年的话——等到自己份额被侵蚀，正说明 Vanguard 的使命成功了，'做减法来得加法'（addition by subtraction）才是 Bogle 毕生的事业。节目回溯指数基金的缘起（Paul Samuelson 的呼吁）、起步时高达 43 个基点的费用如何靠共同持有（mutually owned）结构不断下调，以及 Fidelity 500 Index Fund 以 1 个基点收费做到 8500 亿美元等细节；也点出 Vanguard 占 27% 资产却只贡献行业约 5%–6% 收入的反差。结尾 Balchunas 把 Bogle 比作'朋克摇滚'，并从 70 年代初的市场废墟谈到创造性破坏（creative destruction）的价值，是一集兼具行业史与人物刻画的纪念性对谈。
description: Vanguard’s Plateau Is Exactly What Jack Bogle Wanted

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。

turns.en: Podcasts, radio, news. Bogle in his office in probably 10 years ago, and he wrote a book called Enough. And I remember I was in his office because he has a framed, he had a framed picture of his book, Enough. And then he put Donald Trump's book, Never Enough, next to it. And he goes, you like that? You know, and he was very proud that he was about, he didn't think they needed to grow that much more.
turns.zh: Podcasts、radio、news。大概十年前，Bogle 在他办公室里，他写了一本叫 Enough 的书。我记得我在他的办公室，因为他有一张装裱起来的、他这本 Enough 的书封照片。然后他把 Donald Trump 的书 Never Enough 摆在旁边。他说，你喜欢这样吗？你知道，他很为自己这种态度自豪，他不觉得他们需要再增长多少了。

turns.en: Welcome to Trillions. I'm Joel Weber.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Trillions。我是 Joel Weber。

turns.en: And I'm Eric Belchunis.
turns.zh: 我是 Eric Balchunas。

turns.en: Today, Vanguard is synonymous with passive investing. And on August 31st, the company celebrated the 50th anniversary of the first index fund. But just as the company has reached that milestone, here's the brutal reality. Its market share has actually plateaued. And in 1991, Jack Bogle, Vanguard's founder, even said, if this day ever came, it was a sign of Vanguard's mission succeeding. Who roots for their company to lose market share, Eric?
turns.zh: 今天，Vanguard 已经是被动投资（passive investing）的代名词。而在8月31日，这家公司庆祝了第一只指数基金（index fund）诞生50周年。但就在公司达到这个里程碑之际，残酷的现实是：它的市场份额（market share）其实已经见顶走平了。而在1991年，Vanguard 的创始人 Jack Bogle 甚至说过，如果有一天真到了这个地步，那正说明 Vanguard 的使命成功了。有谁会盼着自己公司丢市场份额呢，Eric？

turns.en: Only a maniac. And that was really Jack Bogle. I mean, he was different. And his whole life, in my opinion, was really about addition by subtraction. And I think that was his life's work more than, say, the index fund.
turns.zh: 只有疯子才会。而那恰恰就是 Jack Bogle。我是说，他与众不同。在我看来，他这一生真正做的，就是做减法来得加法（addition by subtraction）。我觉得这才是他毕生的事业，甚至超过指数基金本身。

turns.en: We're joined by Isabel Lee, a cross-asset reporter with Bloomberg News. This time on Trillions, the Bogle effect. Eric, you guys at Bloomberg Intelligence recently published a note about that I thought was pretty interesting about Vanguard. No surprise, you know a thing or two about Vanguard. You've actually written a book about Bogle, the founder of Vanguard. But this recent research, I think, is pretty important because it reveals that maybe Vanguard's dominance isn't on the ascent anymore.
turns.zh: 今天加入我们的是 Isabel Lee，Bloomberg News 的跨资产（cross-asset）记者。本期 Trillions 的主题是 Bogle 效应（the Bogle effect）。Eric，你们 Bloomberg Intelligence 最近发布了一篇关于 Vanguard 的研究报告，我觉得挺有意思的。这毫不意外，你对 Vanguard 相当了解。你其实还写过一本关于 Vanguard 创始人 Bogle 的书。但我觉得这次的研究相当重要，因为它揭示出，Vanguard 的主导地位也许已经不再上升了。

turns.en: How about that?
turns.zh: 怎么样？

turns.en: Yeah, I was at the 50th anniversary party For the index fund, which just happened recently at the New York Stock Exchange.
turns.zh: 对，我去了指数基金50周年的庆祝派对，就在不久前，在纽约证券交易所（New York Stock Exchange）办的。

turns.en: Vanguard was throwing this party?
turns.zh: 这派对是 Vanguard 办的？

turns.en: Yeah, at the New York Stock Exchange. I mean, everybody's kind of a fan of indexing at this point. It was a Vanguard event for sure because two Vanguard executives spoke. But there was some reporters there, some old timers from back in the day, the Bogleheads folks. So it was a really cool room. I knew a good chunk of people from my Bogle effect book research. And anyway, I was going to write a couple notes on this milestone. What does it mean? Yada, yada. And when I went to pull the chart of Vanguard's market share and their assets, I noticed that it had plateaued. For 50 years, Vanguard's market share went up and up and up and up till they commanded 27% of all fund assets. That's ETF plus mutual funds. But that kind of leveled off and it even trickled down a little. And if you look at BlackRock and Fidelity, they're kind of coming up. But also, there's so many other issuers with so many cheap products. And I thought, oh, this is interesting. And I remember it in my book that Bogle had once said that he'll know that his mission and Vanguard's mission is beginning to be realized when their own market share erodes, which is like insane to say in 1991. But he saw that happening. And it's ironic, or I guess perfect, that it happened exactly 50 years. So I thought it was cool that this anniversary was not just the 50 years of the index, but also Bogle's really grand vision coming true of Vanguard investing. being so influential that everybody else got cheap and started getting their own flows and Vanguard's market share plateaued.
turns.zh: 对，在纽约证券交易所。我是说，现在大家都挺推崇指数化投资（indexing）的。这肯定是场 Vanguard 的活动，因为有两位 Vanguard 的高管发了言。但现场也有一些记者，一些当年的老前辈，还有 Bogleheads 那群人。所以那是个特别酷的场子。我做 Bogle 效应那本书的研究时，认识里面不少人。总之，我本来打算就这个里程碑写几篇笔记。它意味着什么？blah blah。结果当我去调出 Vanguard 市场份额和资产规模的图表时，我注意到它已经见顶走平了。50年来，Vanguard 的市场份额一路涨、涨、涨、涨，直到占据了全部基金资产的27%。这是 ETF 加共同基金（mutual funds）的口径。但之后就基本走平了，甚至还略微往下掉了一点。你看 BlackRock 和 Fidelity，它们正在往上走。而且还有非常多其他发行方，推出大量便宜的产品。我就想，哦，这有意思。我记得我在书里写过，Bogle 曾经说过，等到他们自己的市场份额开始被侵蚀时，他就知道他的使命、Vanguard 的使命开始实现了——在1991年说这话简直是疯了。但他预见到了。而它恰好在整整50年后发生，真是讽刺，或者说，恰到好处。所以我觉得这个周年纪念很酷，它不只是指数基金的50年，更是 Bogle 那个真正宏大的愿景成真：Vanguard 的投资方式影响力大到让其他所有人都变便宜了、开始拿到自己的资金流入，而 Vanguard 自己的市场份额见顶走平了。

turns.en: I actually read that note, Eric.
turns.zh: 我其实读了那篇报告，Eric。

turns.en: And then at the top, you said that it's kind of like Bogle's dream coming true because he wants the whole industry to be low cost. And then I thought, but is it really like, did he envision that it will be like in the US, a $ 13 trillion industry, globally, $ 22 trillion? I mean, maybe it was his dream, but I'm sure his people would want to still keep on dominating. It kind of reminds me of, do you guys know Hinge? I know everyone is married here, but Hinge.
turns.zh: 然后你在开头说，这有点像是 Bogle 的梦想成真，因为他希望整个行业都低成本。然后我就想，但真的是这样吗？他有没有设想过，在美国这会是一个13万亿美元的行业、在全球是22万亿美元？我是说，也许这是他的梦想，但我敢说他那些人还是想继续占据主导。这让我想起——你们知道 Hinge 吗？我知道在座的都结婚了，但 Hinge。

turns.en: Is that like Match.com for Gen Z?
turns.zh: 那是给 Z 世代（Gen Z）用的 Match.com 吗？

turns.en: Yes, sure. The dating app.
turns.zh: 对，没错。就是那个约会软件（dating app）。

turns.en: So its motto is something like the app designed to be deleted. But do you really want to be deleted?
turns.zh: 它的口号大概是'一款生来就该被删掉的 app'。可你真的想被删掉吗？

turns.en: You know what I mean? Well, I mean, do you want to try and find love? Yeah, sure.
turns.zh: 你懂我意思吧？呃，我是说，你想不想努力去找到爱情？想啊，当然。

turns.en: I guess.
turns.zh: 我想是吧。

turns.en: I mean, is the world better that everything is or most things are low cost?
turns.zh: 我是说，如果所有东西、或者大多数东西都低成本了，这个世界会变得更美好吗？

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: I'm happy.
turns.zh: 我挺满意的。

turns.en: How conflicted? is Vanguard about this?
turns.zh: 对于这件事，Vanguard 内心有多纠结？

turns.en: Eric is a great question. This is why I called the book, the Bogle effect and not the Vanguard effect. Joel, I could have sold like five times more copies because when you travel around, A lot of people do not know the word Boggle. They call it Boggle.
turns.zh: 这是个好问题。这正是为什么我把书名叫 Bogle 效应，而不是 Vanguard 效应。Joel，我本来能多卖五倍的册数，因为你到处跑的时候会发现，很多人不认识 Bogle 这个词。他们把它念成 Boggle。

turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 对，完全是。

turns.en: They're like the Boggle effect. Even people in the industry were like, Boggle, that's a word game, I think, from the 80s. Pretty good game, actually. But anyway, Boggle or Boggle the Mind.
turns.zh: 他们会说' Boggle 效应'。连业内的人都会说，Boggle？我记得那是80年代的一个文字游戏吧。其实那游戏还挺好玩的。总之吧，Boggle，或者说 Boggle the Mind。

turns.en: When you play that game, do you call it Boggle when you play it, Aaron?
turns.zh: 你玩那个游戏的时候，会把它叫成 Boggle 吗，Eric？

turns.en: Now I do, yes. But anyway, they called Boggle and this and that. But everybody knows Vanguard, right? Which is testament to Boggle in effect because he really put Vanguard front and center, but I thought he was the anomaly in physics. This particular person was weird and different and on a different trip. Vanguard itself, since Bogle has stepped down as CEO, has done a lot of things he would not do. And he kind of crapped on from his office at the research center. He didn't want them to go into ETFs, although I'd say that was a good idea. He didn't even like international. He didn't like smart beta. They went into the quant world. They went into privates. He wouldn't have liked that. There's been a series of things that they did that he probably would not have done.
turns.zh: 现在我确实这么叫了，是的。总之吧，他们叫它 Boggle 什么的。但人人都知道 Vanguard，对吧？这恰恰证明了 Bogle 效应，因为他真的把 Vanguard 推到了台前正中央，可我觉得他是物理学意义上的异类。这个特定的人很古怪、很不一样，走的是另一条路。Vanguard 自己呢，自从 Bogle 卸任 CEO 之后，做了很多他不会做的事。他就从研究中心的办公室里对这些事一顿吐槽。他不想让他们做 ETF，尽管我得说那是个好主意。他甚至不喜欢国际（international）投资。他不喜欢 smart beta（智能贝塔）。他们进入了量化（quant）领域。他们进入了私募（privates）领域。这些他都不会喜欢。他们做了一系列他大概不会去做的事。

turns.en: Crypto, you're not mentioning.
turns.zh: 还有加密货币（crypto），你没提到。

turns.en: Well, they didn't get into crypto. They simply have a brokerage in which they allow crypto. So I would say that's neutral. I think being anti-crypto, if he ran Vanguard, he probably would still have a ban on crypto trading. He wasn't a fan of crypto or gold. Listen, Bogle basically, I think, was almost like a He started his life as a classic Wall Street active manager, asset manager guy. And he eventually, over 50 years, worked himself into being a Buddhist monk, sitting Indian style for 12 hours a day and eating crickets. It is so hard to get to that level of simplicity where he thought, really, everything is really a distraction. You just want to buy the S & P 500 for three bips and wait 50 years. But not everybody is that Puritan. So that actually put him in odds with his own company. But Vanguard itself, it's still mutually owned. It still has that Boy Scout reputation. But look, now the guy running it is from BlackRock. A lot of people who work there have MBAs where they're taught how to make more money. And you see the way they're launching funds. They're looking to get more assets. And when I saw Vogel in his office probably 10 years ago, I remember he was like, can you believe we have $ 4 trillion in assets? What in the hell do we need all that money for? And he wrote a book called Enough. And I remember I was in his office because he had a framed picture of his book, Enough, and then he put Donald Trump's book, Never Enough, next to it. And he goes, you like that? And he was very proud that he was about, he didn't think they needed to grow that much more. So again, Bogle, very different. But I do think that 99.9% of people who go to Wall Street are like, hey, how can we make more money? How can we get more assets? That's just how you're taught to do it. That's how people are programmed. Bogle was so different. And I think that that's why he would be really happy that it grew this much. There'd be some things he would not be thrilled about. But I think overall, he'd be like, man, we did it. Everybody out there can go to any asset manager now. Let's say you're a Fidelity customer or a BlackRock customer. And you can get a Vanguard-like product, no problem, for most asset classes. So he kind of forced the whole industry to change. So you can say, because some people ask me, why have no other companies structured themselves as mutually owned like Vanguard? And I'm like, they don't have to.
turns.zh: 嗯，他们并没有真正进入加密货币。他们只是有一家券商业务，允许交易加密货币。所以我觉得那是中性的。我认为他是反加密货币的，如果他还执掌 Vanguard，他大概仍会禁止加密货币交易。他不喜欢加密货币，也不喜欢黄金。听着，我觉得 Bogle 基本上几乎是——他人生起步时是个典型的华尔街主动管理型基金经理、资产管理人。而经过50年，他最后把自己修成了一个佛教僧侣，每天盘腿打坐12个小时、吃蟋蟀。要达到那种极简境界太难了，在他那种境界里，他觉得说实话，一切其实都是干扰。你就是想花三个基点（bips）买入 S&P 500，然后等上50年。但并不是每个人都那么清教徒式（Puritan）。所以这反而让他和自己的公司起了冲突。但 Vanguard 本身，它仍然是共同持有（mutually owned）的。它仍然保有那种童子军（Boy Scout）式的好名声。但你看，现在执掌它的人来自 BlackRock。那里很多员工都有 MBA，MBA 教的是怎么赚更多钱。你看他们发行基金的方式就知道了。他们想要拿到更多资产。大概10年前我在 Bogle 办公室见他时，我记得他说，你敢信我们有4万亿美元的资产吗？我们他妈要这么多钱干嘛？他写了一本叫 Enough 的书。我记得我在他的办公室，因为他有一张装裱起来的、他这本 Enough 的书封照片，然后他把 Donald Trump 的书 Never Enough 摆在旁边。他说，你喜欢这样吗？他很为自己这种态度自豪，他不觉得他们需要再增长多少了。所以再说一次，Bogle 非常与众不同。但我确实觉得，去华尔街的人里有99.9%都是想着，嘿，我们怎么才能赚更多钱？怎么才能拿到更多资产？这就是别人教你的做法。人们就是这么被编程的。Bogle 太不一样了。我觉得正因如此，看到它长到这个规模，他会真的很高兴。有些事情他不会那么满意。但我总体上觉得他会说，老兄，我们做到了。现在外面的每个人都可以去找任何一家资产管理公司。假设你是 Fidelity 的客户，或者 BlackRock 的客户。你都能拿到一个类 Vanguard 的产品，没问题，涵盖大多数资产类别。所以他相当于逼着整个行业改变了。所以你可以说——因为有人问我，为什么没有其他公司像 Vanguard 那样把自己设计成共同持有的结构？我就说，他们没必要这么做。

turns.en: They already are.
turns.zh: 他们本来就已经是这样了。

turns.en: They're basically governed by this force to a degree. And it is just a crazy, again, anomaly that we have. are witnessing that is still rippling out.
turns.zh: 他们在某种程度上其实都被这股力量支配着。而这又是一个疯狂的、我们说过的异类，我们正在见证它，它的涟漪还在不断扩散。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: So rewind the clock back 50 years. That was when the first index investment trust launched Vanguard launched that. And, and that that's the fund that is celebrating its 50th anniversary. Only that's now the Vanguard 500 index fund. How radical was the first index investment trust in 1976 era?
turns.zh: 那我们把时钟拨回50年前。那时第一只指数投资信托（index investment trust）发行，是 Vanguard 推出的。而那正是现在庆祝50周年的这只基金。只不过它现在叫 Vanguard 500 Index Fund。在1976年那个年代，第一只指数投资信托有多激进？

turns.en: Very radical. Now, he got the idea from reading a trade publication. I think it was called the Portfolio Management Index or publication, one of those journals. And in there, Paul Samuelson, I believe that's his name, who actually worked in the Kennedy administration, there was some buzz about active managers maybe not being as good as advertised. And Paul Samuelson in there said, hey, can someone please launch an index fund so we can grade these active managers? And Bogle, who had just set up Vanguard as a back office company, it was not allowed to run money, because of a situation with his old colleagues, he was like, wait, why don't we do it? It's not running money because it's an index fund. Let's try it. And that's how the idea was born, more out of necessity, really, than any grand vision. So he launched it. And I think the real bold part was, A, nobody had tried to actually put an index fund into action. There were indexes, but not funds, really. There was one tiny attempt before. But long story short, it was really a new idea. The big thing, I think, that made it unusual was there was no distribution fees. So at that time, it was very, very normal. and standard to pay a broker a load to put the client in there. And so without that load, the brokers weren't incentivized to use your fund. And so Bogle kind of set this up outside of the whole system. And my metaphor with this would be like, let's say, Isabelle made the greatest movie ever made, like something like as good as The Odyssey or whatever. But she would not show it in any movie theater. And she wouldn't let Netflix or HBO or any of those distribution channels have it. You had to go to her backyard to watch it. You know, and I say that movie better be damn good.
turns.zh: 非常激进。他是从一份行业刊物上得到的这个想法。我记得那叫 Portfolio Management Index 之类的刊物，是那种期刊之一。在里面，Paul Samuelson——我记得是这个名字，他其实在 Kennedy 政府里任过职——当时有些议论，说主动管理型基金经理也许没有宣传的那么厉害。Paul Samuelson 在里面说，嘿，能不能有人推出一只指数基金，好让我们给这些主动基金经理打个分？而 Bogle 当时刚把 Vanguard 设立成一家后台运营公司，因为和他老同事之间的一些情况，它是不被允许管理资金的。他就想，等等，我们为什么不做呢？这不算主动管理资金，因为它是指数基金。我们试试吧。这个想法就这样诞生了，与其说是出于什么宏大愿景，不如说更多是出于现实需要。于是他推出了它。我觉得真正大胆的地方在于：第一，之前没人真正尝试过把一只指数基金落地运作。有指数，但基本没有对应的基金。之前有过一次很小的尝试。但长话短说，这真的是个新想法。我觉得让它显得不同寻常的关键，是它没有分销费（distribution fees）。在那个年代，付给经纪人一笔销售佣金（load）、把客户塞进基金里，是非常非常普遍和标准的做法。所以没有那笔佣金，经纪人就没有动力去卖你的基金。于是 Bogle 相当于把这套东西架在了整个体系之外。我对此的比喻是这样的：比如说，Isabel 拍出了有史以来最伟大的电影，好比跟 The Odyssey 一样好或者什么的。但她不会在任何电影院上映它。她也不会让 Netflix、HBO 或任何那些发行渠道拿到它。你必须去她家后院才能看。你知道，而我会说，那部电影最好他妈的很好看。

turns.en: How much are you charging?
turns.zh: 那你打算收多少钱？

turns.en: First of all, there's no backyard in New York.
turns.zh: 首先，纽约根本没有后院。

turns.en: Maybe Joel has a backyard. But that's a nice analogy.
turns.zh: 也许 Joel 有个后院。不过这比喻挺不错的。

turns.en: Another thing that you mentioned, Eric, when we talked last week, because I wrote about this in the newsletter was, okay, it's radical when the fund launched, but it wasn't until they started really whittling down the fee that it gathered assets. Because when it first launched, it had something like a 43 basis point fee, which is kind of high in today's world. And it wasn't until they made it just two basis points, eventually becoming one basis point, which is dirt cheap, that it really gathered funds. And I feel like to your point, that's really the ethos of Vanguard, which is extremely low cost.
turns.zh: 还有一点你上周我们聊的时候提到过，Eric，因为我在通讯（newsletter）里写过：好吧，基金刚发行时是很激进，但直到他们开始真正一点点把费用削下来，它才聚集起资产。因为它刚发行时，费用大概是43个基点（basis point），以今天的世界来看算是挺高的。直到他们把它降到只有两个基点、最终变成一个基点——那是极便宜了——它才真正聚集起资金。我觉得正如你说的，那才是 Vanguard 真正的精神内核，也就是极低成本。

turns.en: But even 43 basis points was probably way cheaper than whatever the.
turns.zh: 但即便是43个基点，大概也远比当时那些——

turns.en: Active funds were at the time, right?
turns.zh: 主动型基金当时的收费便宜得多，对吧？

turns.en: That is true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.en: Yeah. People don't know that it started life at 43. They think it was born at like five and it just wasn't. It was the mutual ownership structure that every time it got some assets and they had extra profit, the board, which is made up of the investors, voted to lower fees because it was their funds. They wanted lower fees and not to endorse or say, sponsor a stadium or pay people more, executives more money. So that mutual ownership structure kept lowering the fee from 43 to 40 to 35. It wasn't until like the 90s that it got to 20. And that's when the flows even started. Like it was 20 years, nobody cared that much. Bogle was really out there just trying to get people to listen for a long time. Again, he's outside of the system, which makes it hard. So around 95-ish, it got below 20. That's when flows started to come in. but they still weren't hot and heavy. And at 95, that's when Vogel stepped down as CEO, index mutual funds have $ 22 trillion in assets. 99.8% of their assets have come in after 1995. So that means for 20 years, they only got 0.2% of the assets they have today. So that tells you how hard it was to get this going. And then in the 2008-ish period, a bunch of things came together that made this trend explode. One, the fees got below 10. That's big. Because a 40 basis, 40 index fund is pretty good. But a free index fund, basically, that's hot stuff. Then 2008, active managers didn't sidestep the great financial crisis. They all went down as much or more than the market. So people are like, why am I paying all this money for this manager? I'll just go vanguard. And then the third thing was the internet really started to spread in the mid-outs, right? They Everybody started getting internet connection. And when you got the spread of information, more people were aware of like costs and long-term returns. It was hard to get this information up until then. So those three things all kind of hit and kicked in around 2008, 2009. And that's when you see the index assets go parabolic. And that's when it really took off. So again, it took 30 years to get to that point. And that's why the Bogle is an interesting story because he purposely would take the harder road. No distribution fees. really delayed the success for many years, but he knew it would give the investor a better deal.
turns.zh: 对。人们不知道它起步时是43个基点。他们以为它生来就是五个基点左右，其实不是。正是共同持有的结构，每当它拿到一些资产、有了额外利润，由投资者组成的董事会就投票降低费用，因为那是他们自己的基金。他们想要更低的费用，而不是去代言、比如说赞助一座体育场，或者给高管们发更多钱。所以那种共同持有的结构不断把费用从43降到40、再降到35。一直到大概90年代才降到20。而那才是资金流入真正开始的时候。也就是说有20年，几乎没人在意。Bogle 真的长期在外面，就是努力想让人们听进去。再说一次，他游离在体系之外，这让事情很难。所以大约在95年前后，费用降到了20以下。那时资金开始流入，但还不算火爆。而在95年，那正是 Bogle 卸任 CEO 的时候，指数共同基金如今有22万亿美元的资产。他们99.8%的资产都是1995年之后才进来的。这意味着在此之前的20年里，他们只拿到了今天所拥有资产的0.2%。这就告诉你，把这件事推动起来有多难。然后在2008年前后那段时间，一系列因素凑到一起，让这个趋势爆发。第一，费用降到了10以下。这很关键。因为一个40基点的指数基金已经相当不错了。但一只基本免费的指数基金，那才是香饽饽。然后2008年，主动基金经理们并没有躲过那场大金融危机（great financial crisis）。他们全都跌得和市场一样多、甚至更多。所以人们就想，我为什么要为这个基金经理付这么多钱？我干脆去 Vanguard 好了。第三件事是，互联网在2000年代中期真正开始普及，对吧？大家都开始能上网。而当信息传播开来，更多人意识到了成本和长期回报这些概念。在那之前，这些信息是很难获取的。所以这三件事都在2008、2009年前后集中爆发、开始起作用。那时你就看到指数资产呈抛物线式飙升。那才是它真正腾飞的时候。所以再说一次，走到那一步花了30年。这也是为什么 Bogle 是个有意思的故事，因为他会刻意选择那条更难的路。不收分销费，真的把成功推迟了很多年，但他知道这会给投资者一个更好的交易条件。

turns.en: And he also built a better mousetrap. He built a better mousetrap.
turns.zh: 而且他还造了一个更好的捕鼠器（mousetrap）。他造了一个更好的捕鼠器。

turns.en: Yes. And also, again, as you know, Joel, we wrote this article comparing Vogel to punk rock, because I do think at the end of the day that, you know, Indexing needed Vanguard more than Vanguard needed indexing. What Vogel's story is really about is addition by subtraction. Let's take the fees out, expense ratio. Let's remove the trading costs because indexes don't trade that much. So there's not that much fees from the portfolio turning over like with active funds. Let's also remove brokers. He wanted you to just like not use a broker and go right to Vanguard to your backyard, to the backyard metaphor. And that would be, and also he wanted to solve the behavioral issue. Stop buying high and selling low on your emotions. Just marry this index fund and don't look at it for 50 years. So by really, I guess, removing all of these bad things, he created like the ultimate mousetrap, in my opinion. And that's his life's work. And it's much more complicated than the index fund. It's really about addition by subtraction.
turns.zh: 对。而且，再说一次，如你所知，Joel，我们写过一篇文章把 Bogle 比作朋克摇滚（punk rock），因为我确实觉得，说到底，指数化投资需要 Vanguard，胜过 Vanguard 需要指数化投资。Bogle 的故事真正讲的就是做减法来得加法。我们把费用拿掉——费用率（expense ratio）。我们把交易成本去掉，因为指数不怎么换手交易。所以不会像主动型基金那样，因为组合频繁换手产生那么多费用。我们再把经纪人去掉。他就是希望你干脆别用经纪人，直接去找 Vanguard、去他家后院，用那个后院的比喻来说。而且他还想解决行为上的问题。别再凭着情绪高买低卖了。就跟这只指数基金'结婚'，50年都别看它。所以通过——我猜——真正把这些坏东西全都去掉，他造出了那个终极的捕鼠器，在我看来。那才是他毕生的事业。它比指数基金本身复杂得多。它真正讲的是做减法来得加法。

turns.zh: 这就是一个完美的赚钱小工具，也是拥抱资本主义的方式。这也正是资金流入之所以是那个样子的原因。不过 Eric，把话题拉回到市场份额这件事上。如果 Vanguard 已经见顶走平，那对 Vanguard 和整个行业来说意味着什么？

turns.en: And why have they plateaued, Eric?

turns.en: Yeah, well, let me give you an example. Fidelity, that was their biggest competitor in the 80s. Good trivia, by the way, for anybody out there. What was the last two biggest funds on planet Earth before Vanguard Total Market took over? The answer is Bill Gross' PIMCO total return, and then before that, Fidelity Magellan. So those two active funds. Yeah, Magellan in particular.
turns.zh: 嗯，好，我举个例子。Fidelity，那是他们80年代最大的竞争对手。顺便说个不错的冷知识，给外面任何人。在 Vanguard Total Market 接管之前，地球上最大的两只基金是什么？答案是 Bill Gross 的 PIMCO Total Return，再往前，是 Fidelity Magellan。就是那两只主动型基金。对，尤其是 Magellan。

turns.zh: 这两只里哪只更大？

turns.en: Bill Gross is, but remember, a billion isn't what it used to be. As the years go on, you have to inflation adjust, really. But they were both monsters. And anybody who was alive, anybody over 45 probably remembers the Fidelity Magellan. It was all over the Wall Street Journal all the time. Whatever the portfolio manager was doing was a big deal. That was Peter Lynch's fund. People remember his name.
turns.zh: Bill Gross 那只更大，但要记住，十亿美元已经不像当年那么值钱了。随着年头过去，你真的得做通胀调整。但它们两个都是巨无霸。任何还在世的人、任何45岁以上的人大概都记得 Fidelity Magellan。它当时铺天盖地上 Wall Street Journal。那位投资组合经理做什么都是一件大事。那是 Peter Lynch 的基金。人们记得他的名字。

turns.en: Yeah, it's still a big deal now.
turns.zh: 对，即便现在也仍是大事。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So anyway- Fidelity, their biggest fund today is the Fidelity 500 Index Fund that charges one basis point, has $ 850 billion. Wow. That's four times bigger than any other fund they have. So that just tells you how powerful Vanguard's concept was. And Fidelity even puts out press releases saying, hey, we're actually cheaper than Vanguard, which is like, wow, the world has turned. That's where we're at. So Fidelity doesn't exactly love that you love that fund, though, because it only makes one basis point.
turns.zh: 总之——Fidelity，他们今天最大的基金是 Fidelity 500 Index Fund，收一个基点的费用，规模有8500亿美元。哇。这比他们其他任何一只基金都大四倍。这就说明 Vanguard 的理念有多强大。Fidelity 甚至发新闻稿说，嘿，我们其实比 Vanguard 还便宜——这简直是，哇，世道变了。这就是我们现在的处境。所以 Fidelity 其实并不那么乐意你这么喜欢那只基金，因为它只赚一个基点。

turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: To be fair to Vanguard, they want you in the cheap stuff. A lot of other people do it because they have to, because their customers are like, I'm going to go somewhere else if I can't get cheap beta with you. Then that company will be like, okay, have your core beta, but use us for some ancillary satellite positions and maybe hot sauce, and we can make some more money there or use our advisory service or a brokerage platform. So they just try to upsell you and do some other things with you that make them money. But these index funds have become a loss leader. You almost have to have them.
turns.zh: 说句公道话，对 Vanguard 来说，他们是真心想让你买便宜的产品。很多其他公司这么做是因为不得不做，因为他们的客户会说，如果我在你这儿拿不到便宜的贝塔（beta），我就去别家了。于是那家公司就会说，好吧，你的核心贝塔拿去，但用我们来做一些辅助性的卫星仓位、也许来点'辣酱'（指高风险高收益产品），我们在那上面能多赚点钱，或者用我们的顾问服务、或者券商平台。所以他们就是想向你追加销售（upsell）、跟你做点别的能让他们赚钱的事。但这些指数基金已经成了一种引流亏本产品（loss leader）。你几乎不得不提供它们。

turns.en: I've thought about this. I personally think at three basis points, maybe they go one lower because SPYM now is two. And that actually just helped close. That's it. It was four S & P 500 ETFs. Anyway, you can get one. I mean, Bank of New York has a zero fee fund, but it is not the S & P 500. Long story short, there's a couple funds below three basis points. So it is already there. I think Vanguard, their reputation is so strong. And people, I think, generally want to pay something. I don't think the zero fee thing is that actually attractive. Ironically, I think it feels gimmicky. So I think like three basis points is like perfect for people or two. I think also Vanguard is using some of their money towards their tech and their customer service. Because here's another stat that's mind-blowing. They have 27% market share of fund assets, but only 5%, 6% of revenue of the industry. So they don't make a lot of money because they charge so little, and they don't have a lot of money for good customer service. So there's been some complaints about long lines and stuff. So there's been pressure on the new management to make better tech, better customer service. And I think that's where I think even their customers would rather them spend money right now. But they might go to two. You might see Vu at two basis points, especially since buy-in cut. But the other thing back to Jules, what do other people do? We have this thing called the Jack Bogle paradox, where the more money that goes into the low-cost passive, whether it's Vanguard or other people, the more exotic the new launches get, which is ironic, right? And that's why you see all these crazy ETF launches, because I think people have a cowboy account that they want to just go wild in, or you have younger people who are looking to gamble and stuff and So that is another way that I think the Bogle effect has changed different things. It's sort of made other people, if you're competing for the core active or index, you got to get cheap. So it's made like core stuff get cheaper. And alternative, it's made people innovate more on the crazy stuff. And I think that's sort of how what he did has actually almost like made everybody orbit around it in different ways. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我想了想这个。我个人觉得在三个基点这个水平上，也许他们会再降一个基点，因为 SPYM 现在是两个基点。而且那其实刚刚帮着收在了那个位置。就是这样。当时是四只 S&P 500 ETF。总之，你能拿到一个。我是说，Bank of New York 有一只零费用的基金，但它不是 S&P 500。长话短说，有几只基金低于三个基点。所以那个价位其实已经到了。我觉得 Vanguard，他们的声誉太强了。而且人们，我觉得，通常是愿意付一点钱的。我不觉得零费用那套真的有那么吸引人。讽刺的是，我觉得它反而显得像个噱头。所以我觉得三个基点、或者两个基点，对人们来说就正好。我还觉得 Vanguard 正在把他们的一部分钱投到技术和客户服务上。因为这里还有一个令人震惊的数据。他们占基金资产的27%市场份额，却只占整个行业收入的5%、6%。所以他们赚的钱不多，因为收费太少，他们也没有很多钱去做好客户服务。所以一直有人抱怨排队久之类的问题。所以新管理层面临着压力，要把技术做得更好、客户服务做得更好。我觉得那才是眼下连他们的客户都更希望他们把钱花上去的地方。但他们可能会降到两个基点。你可能会看到 VOO 降到两个基点，尤其是自从有对手降费以来。但另一点，回到 Joel 的问题，其他人怎么办？我们有一个说法叫 Jack Bogle 悖论（Jack Bogle paradox）：进入低成本被动产品的钱越多——不管是 Vanguard 还是别家——新发行的产品就越花哨，这很讽刺，对吧？这也是为什么你看到这么多疯狂的 ETF 发行，因为我觉得人们有一个'牛仔账户'（cowboy account），就想在里面放开手脚乱来，或者有一些年轻人就是想赌一把之类的。所以我觉得那是 Bogle 效应改变各种事情的另一种方式。它某种程度上让其他人——如果你要争夺核心的主动型或指数型业务，你就得把价格做低。所以它让核心产品变得更便宜了。而另一方面，它让人们在那些疯狂的产品上创新得更多。我觉得这大致就是他做的事，如何几乎让所有人都以不同的方式围着它转。对。

turns.en: I think your book is the perfect title, The Bogle Effect, because we really see the ripple effects until today. But do you think that if Jack Bogle was a millennial, like would his business model or belief or ethos, would it have survived? Because now a part of me thinks, I mean, you said it yourself in the note and facts back it up that their dominance is plateauing. Let's not use eroding, just plateauing. Because there's such immense competition in this space now.
turns.zh: 我觉得你那本书的书名起得再合适不过了，The Bogle Effect，因为我们真的能看到它的涟漪效应一直延续到今天。但你觉得，如果 Jack Bogle 是个千禧一代（millennial），他的商业模式、他的信念或精神内核，还能存活下来吗？因为现在我有一部分想法是——我是说，你自己在报告里也讲了，事实也印证了——他们的主导地位正在见顶走平。我们别用'被侵蚀'，就用'见顶走平'。因为这个领域现在的竞争实在太激烈了。

turns.en: So.
turns.zh: 所以。

turns.en: What if he launched... Jack Bogle was a millennial, I don't think. Do you think it would have been possible for him to succeed?
turns.zh: 如果他是从……假如 Jack Bogle 是个千禧一代，我不这么认为。你觉得他还有可能成功吗？

turns.en: Probably. You know, I just think Jack Bogle was miscast on Wall Street. I just think he probably would have made a better preacher, maybe even like an actor. I mean, I just think he wanted... He was more after adoration than money. And I think once he locked into this St. Jack concept of saving everybody money.
turns.zh: 大概可以吧。你知道，我只是觉得 Jack Bogle 在华尔街被放错了位置。我只是觉得他大概会成为一个更好的布道者，甚至也许像个演员。我是说，我只是觉得他想要……他追求的是别人的敬仰，而不是钱。我觉得一旦他锁定了这个'St. Jack'（圣杰克）式替所有人省钱的定位。

turns.en: He really.
turns.zh: 他就真的

turns.en: leaned into it. And he didn't really, money didn't drive him. His son said he wore the same khakis for like 40 years. He was one of those dudes. He's a lot like Buffett, ironically. But I think making things cheaper for people is always going to work, especially if it's good quality. I mean, Amazon came along, and to me is similar to Vanguard in some ways, in that you can get really anything quickly, cheaply, and people feel like it's a good deal. It's hard to compete with that. So I think he could have existed in any era, but If you read the story, the 60s blew up, and he learned a lot of lessons. And that's why when he restarted his career in the early 70s, he had a good amount of information to do it differently. And so some of this story is circumstantial. So I don't know if you could have dropped him in this environment with the bull market going crazy. Would he say, let's get cheap funds? I don't think he could have because he didn't think of that idea in the 60s when everything was going well. It took a complete market crisis, which is why I have another book project idea, which I have a long list, but one of them is called The Early 70s. I think it makes the case for creative destruction. The Fed and everybody wants to keep stocks up in the economy, and they just print money to keep everything kosher. I think if you let things just blow up sometimes, it's good. It clears out the crap, and what rises up is some good stuff. In the early 70s, we saw changes in culture and business, and a lot of those things have lasted because they came out of the rubble of the blow up of the 60s, both economically and culturally, there was a lot of bloat.
turns.zh: 全身心投入了进去。而且他其实并不、钱并不能驱动他。他儿子说他40年来一直穿同一条卡其裤。他就是那种人。讽刺的是，他跟 Buffett 很像。但我觉得，替人们把东西变便宜，永远都会奏效，尤其是当质量还好的时候。我是说，Amazon 出现了，在我看来某些方面跟 Vanguard 很像，就是你能又快又便宜地买到几乎任何东西，而且人们觉得这是笔划算的买卖。这很难与之竞争。所以我觉得他在任何时代都能存在。但如果你去读那段故事，60年代崩了，他从中学到了很多教训。这也是为什么当他在70年代初重启职业生涯时，他掌握了足够多的信息，可以换一种做法。所以这个故事里有一部分是环境造就的。所以我不知道，如果你把他空投到现在这个牛市疯狂的环境里，他会不会说，我们来搞便宜的基金吧？我觉得他不会，因为在60年代一切都顺风顺水的时候，他并没有想出那个点子。那需要一场彻底的市场危机——这也是为什么我还有另一个书的选题，我有一长串，但其中一个叫 The Early 70s。我觉得它论证了创造性破坏（creative destruction）的价值。美联储（The Fed）和所有人都想让股市和经济往上走，他们就靠印钞来让一切看起来没问题。我觉得有时候如果你就任由事情崩掉，反而是好事。它清除了那些垃圾，而后从废墟中升起来的，是一些好东西。在70年代初，我们看到了文化和商业上的变革，其中很多东西都延续了下来，因为它们是从60年代那场崩溃的瓦砾中诞生的——无论是经济上还是文化上，当时都有大量的浮华冗余。

turns.en: And so I just think that's why we're going to get this playlist to you with some Ramones.
turns.zh: 所以我就觉得，这就是为什么我们要给你做这个歌单，里面放上一些 the Ramones。

turns.en: Eric has so many books in him. I have zero books in me, honestly.
turns.zh: Eric 肚子里能写出好多本书。说实话，我肚子里一本都写不出来。

turns.en: Well, we'll see. I think there's a couple of things that get you going. We can get that.
turns.zh: 嗯，走着瞧吧。我觉得有几件事能让你有话可说。我们可以搞定。

turns.en: We will go over there now.
turns.zh: 我们回头就往那边做。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Isabel, thanks for joining us on Trillions.
turns.zh: Isabel，谢谢你来做客 Trillions。

turns.en: Always a pleasure. If you don't invite me back, I'll take offense.
turns.zh: 一直很荣幸。如果你们不再请我回来，我可会生气的。

turns.en: Don't worry, you're coming back.
turns.zh: 别担心，你会回来的。

turns.en: Thanks for listening to Trillions. Until next time, you can find us on the Bloomberg Terminal, Bloomberg.com, Apple Podcasts, Spotify.
turns.zh: 感谢收听 Trillions。下期再会，你可以在 Bloomberg Terminal、Bloomberg.com、Apple Podcasts、Spotify 上找到我们。

turns.en: Or wherever else you like to listen. We'd love to hear from you. Hit us up on social.
turns.zh: 或者任何你喜欢收听的地方。我们很想听到你的反馈。在社交媒体上联系我们吧。

turns.en: Trillions is produced by Magnus Hendriksen and Keshav Pandya. Amy Keene is our executive producer. Cheryl Brumley is the head of Bloomberg Podcasts.
turns.zh: Trillions 由 Magnus Hendriksen 和 Keshav Pandya 制作。Amy Keene 是我们的执行制作人。Cheryl Brumley 是 Bloomberg Podcasts 的负责人。

turns.en: Bye.
turns.zh: 再见。
